say: Good morning, inquirers! Today we are frogs on a very long number strip.
A frog never jumps at random. Its jumps follow a rule. Our job is to notice the rule, test it with a counter, check our answer and explain why.
Everybody stand up. When I say a number that is in our pattern, STOMP. When it is not, whisper it.
Ready? We count in 2s. Zero, two, four…
Before we hop, I want a prediction. Frog 1 jumps in 4s. Frog 2 jumps in 5s. Will they ever land on the same number?
Thumbs up for yes, sideways for maybe, down for no. Now write your prediction at the top of your strip.
stuck: Stuck on the strip: put your counter on 0 and say “four, eight” out loud as you hop.
Losing track: write each landing under the strip: 4, 8, 12 …
For pairs who want more: ask “Frog 3 jumps in 10s. Where will it meet frog 1?”

say: “Look at the table. The numbers are 2, 8, 14, 20. I notice they go up. How much from 2 to 8? Six. From 8 to 14? Six. From 14 to 20? Six. I check every pair of neighbours and it is always six.”
“So my rule is add 6. To find the 5th number I add 6 to the 4th: 20 + 6 = 26.”
“Now look at the numbers that go down. If they get smaller, my rule is take away. Always check: does my rule work on the last pair too?”

do: Point to a number and ask: “How do you know this number is in the pattern?”
Ask: “What is the jump size? Show me on the strip.”
Ask: “Check your rule on the last pair as well. Does it still work?”
stuck: Hint 1: “Look at two neighbours. How far apart are they?”
Hint 2: “Hop your counter and count each hop out loud.”
Hint 3: do the first one together, then let the child do the next one alone.

say: “Who would like to tell us numbers that both frogs landed on?”
“Why do the numbers both frogs share all end in 0?”
ask: “Who would like to tell us numbers that both frogs landed on?”
Jumps of 5 land on numbers ending in 0 or 5. Jumps of 4 always land on even numbers. A number that is both must end in 0.

say: “Today you noticed a rule, tested it with a counter and explained why. That is what an inquirer does.”
“Take your inquiry journal and I will stamp it when you hand me your exit ticket.”

routine.note: Show this slide for 30 seconds in Lesson 1 and name only the four phases: warm-up, explore, teach, worksheet. Do not read the table. Refer back to it in Lesson 2; after that children know the routine. Online: ask children to keep materials and the workbook beside them from the first minute. The times on the slide are the usual lesson; in Lesson 1 everything before the worksheet starts 2 minutes later because the opening takes 4 minutes. Clock checks (say them to yourself): minute 14 (end of sneak-peek puzzles), minute 42 (start of worksheet) and minute 72. If you are more than 2 minutes behind at the worksheet, use the skip list in the tutor guide; never shorten the worksheet below 28 minutes. Never drop the camera and privacy moment, the look-back or the “you can pass” lines.

rules.note: Read the four rules aloud together. Come back to this slide whenever a child is stuck: which rule could help?

l1-title.note: Objective: Skip count in 2s, 3s and 5s; find and state an add or take-away rule; notice numbers that both counting patterns share. Materials: Paper number strip 0 to 50 (or floor tape), counters, two crayons. Online: Slide number line the tutor can mark on; each child uses a paper strip and a pencil. Parents cut out and tape the number strip before the lesson. Time plan: opening 0 to 4, warm-up 4 to 10 (game 4 to 8, quick questions 8 to 10; ask questions 1 to 3, and 4 and 5 only if you are on time), sneak-peek puzzles 10 to 14, explore 14 to 28, teaching 28 to 38 (click to reveal each step and answer), brain break 38 to 42, worksheet 42 to 72 with short teaching before each page and a check-together slide after it (the last 4 minutes check page 2, after a 1-minute stand-up stretch), talk time 72 to 79, exit ticket 79 to 85, look-back 85 to 88, then flex time and goodbye 88 to 90 (this is the buffer: if you are behind, use it; do not start anything new). Think harder, Go further and the Investigation are for every child to choose, any time or at home. Nobody is told which page they should be on.

l1-warm1.note: Minutes 4 to 8. Skip-count stomp: count in 2s, 5s and 3s as a class. Clap on every multiple, whisper on the rest.

l1-warm2.note: Minutes 8 to 10. Read each question aloud, give thinking time, take answers, then click to show the answer. For 4 ask: "Are we going up or down? So do we add or take away?" For 5, children can hop it on the number strip: 4 jumps of 5 land on 20, 4 jumps of 3 land on 12. Answers: 1) 8 2) 15 3) 12 4) 16 5) jumps of 5 (20 is further than 12). Ask questions 1 to 3. Ask 4 and 5 only if the clock at minute 8 is on time. The 4-minute sneak-peek puzzles follow on the next slide.

l1-warmcheck.note: Minutes 10 to 14 (4 minutes). SAY (about 26 words, once): "Two sneak-peek puzzles: ideas we have not learnt yet. A guess is a great start, and I do not know is welcome. Nobody is marked." Question 1 is an access question: every child can try it with objects, a drawing or counting, so everyone starts with a win. Question 2 makes you think. Children try both on their own paper (about a minute each). Then everyone shows their paper ONCE, after the second question: face to face, each child holds the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, everyone holds the paper to the camera at the same moment. There are no private chat messages. Never use boards held up in front of the group, and never read out or compare anyone's answer. Do not write scores down or announce them. Then click to show each answer to the whole group and say "Lots of us had a different idea, and that is fine." Look for good ideas to praise in a later lesson; do not keep a list of who found question 2 easy. When the worksheet starts (minute 42) invite the WHOLE group (“When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation”), never one child by name. Everyone joins Explore and the Mini-lesson. Answers: 1) 12. Hop on 3 more from 9: 10, 11, 12. 2) No. It lands on 19, then 22, so it jumps over 20. (Keep hopping, or notice it only lands on numbers that are 1 more than a 3s number.)

l1-explore1.note: Minutes 14 to 19. Pairs work with the materials: Paper number strip 0 to 50 (or floor tape), counters, two crayons. Pairs hop a counter along the number strip: frog 1 in 4s, frog 2 in 5s. Mark where each lands. Which numbers do both frogs land on? Online: Slide number line the tutor can mark on; each child uses a paper strip and a pencil. The number strip is cut out and taped before the lesson (parents are asked in the materials message), so no cutting is needed in class. The number strip is cut out and taped before the lesson (parents are asked in the materials message), so no cutting is needed in class. The number strip is cut out and taped before the lesson (parents are asked in the materials message), so no cutting is needed in class. Go further (what-if) is on this slide from the start: any pair may choose it at any time, so nobody waits. The tutor does not choose who and does not announce it. Answers: 20 and 40 (frog 1 lands on 4, 8, ... 48; frog 3 on 10, 20, 30, 40, 50).

l1-explore2.note: Minutes 19 to 28. Let pairs keep working and move around the room (or breakout rooms). Gather them to answer these. Answers: 1) 20 and 40 (and 0). 2) We say them when we count in 20s: 20 is 5 jumps of 4 and also 4 jumps of 5. 3) Both frogs still land on 20 and 40.

l1-teach1.note: Teach. Point at 2 and 8 and ask: "How far is it from 2 to 8?" Count the hops on the strip with the children: 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. Six hops. Click to show +6. Then ask the same for 8 to 14 and 14 to 20, clicking after each. Click 4 shows the next jump and 26. Think-aloud: "The numbers are 2, 8, 14, 20. They go up. How much from 2 to 8? Six. From 8 to 14? Six. From 14 to 20? Six. I check every pair of neighbours and it is always six. So my rule is add 6. The next number is 20 + 6 = 26." Watch for children who count the numbers in between (3, 4, 5, 6, 7 is five numbers) instead of counting the hops (six). Show them: put a finger on 2, then say a number for every hop.

l1-we1.note: Click to reveal each step. Before each click, ask the group to predict it. Many children say "yes" to 30 because it "feels close". Ask: "How can we test it?" Think-aloud: "My rule is add 6. 26 + 6 = 32. The pattern lands on 26 and then on 32. It never lands on 30, so 30 is not in the pattern. Is 38 in it? 32 + 6 = 38, yes." Count on from 26 on the strip if children are unsure: 27, 28, 29, 30, 31, 32.

l1-try1.note: Children write on their own paper or whiteboard. Nobody holds a board up in front of the group: face to face, each child holds the paper low so only the tutor sees it; online, each child holds the paper to the camera at the same moment, or shows only the tutor. Click for each answer. a) Add 4: 13 + 4 = 17, 17 + 4 = 21. b) The numbers go down, so take away 3: 25 − 3 = 22. Anyone who writes 28 has added: ask "Are the numbers getting bigger or smaller?" c) Add 5: 19, 24, 29, 34. It jumps from 29 to 34, so 30 is not in the pattern.

l1-we2.note: Click through the steps. Stress step 2: only use two numbers that sit next to each other. 36 and 28 are not neighbours, there is a gap between them. Think-aloud: "The numbers are getting smaller, so my rule is take away. From 40 to 36 I count back 4. Take away 4. 36 − 4 = 32. Then 32 − 4 = 28, and 28 is already there, so my rule works. 28 − 4 = 24 and 24 − 4 = 20, which is there too. My rule is take away 4." Common slip: writing "add 4" because the jump is 4. Ask: "Up or down?"

l1-try2.note: Own paper, shown only to the tutor. a) Take away 5 (50 to 45): 45 − 5 = 40, 35 − 5 = 30. b) The neighbours we know are 11 and 15: add 4. 3 + 4 = 7, check 7 + 4 = 11, then 15 + 4 = 19. c) Take away 2: 21, 19. Ask a child who got b right to explain which two numbers they used.

l1-key.note: Say the key idea together. Common mistakes to watch for during the worksheet: (1) Counting the numbers in between instead of the hops: from 4 to 7 they count "5, 6" and say the jump is 2. Put a finger on 4 and say a number for every hop: 5, 6, 7 is 3 hops. (2) Writing "add 3" when the numbers go down (it is take away 3). (3) Restarting the count from 0 instead of adding to the last number. (4) Q4: missing 50, or listing numbers only one child says.

l1-break.note: Four minutes. Online: children stay in view of the camera and move in place.

l1-ws1.note: Minutes 42 to 52. Pairs work together. Walk around and ask "How do you know?" before giving any help. Q2b goes down: check that pairs write take away. Q3 is like the frog explore, but on a shorter line. At minute 42 read questions 1 and 2 aloud, then pairs read the rest. The workbook says: "After question 3 you may choose: carry on, or try Think harder." Never announce who is on which page and never name a child in front of the group; invite the WHOLE group at once, for example: "When you have finished Start here, you can choose Think harder, Go further or the Investigation." Do not split a pair unless both children agree.

l1-ws1ans.note: Click each answer after a pair explains theirs. Q2b: ask "How did you know it was take away?" (the numbers get smaller). Q3: ask a child to hop both frogs on the class number line.

l1-teachboth.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q4 uses counting in 2s and in 5s, so we practise with 2s and 3s here; do not do 2s and 5s for them). Write the two lists on the board one under the other and ring the matches. Think-aloud: "I write the 2s in a row. Then I write the 3s under them. Now I look for numbers that are in both rows: 6, 12, 18." Ask: "Is 9 in both? No, we do not say 9 when we count in 2s."

l1-teachtable.note: Teach before worksheet page 2 (Q5, the sticker boxes). Click to fill the stickers row; say each step aloud: "1, add 4 is 5. 5, add 4 is 9 …" Common mistake: adding 4 to the box number (box 2 has 2 + 4 = 6). Then the odd and even reminder. Here every number is odd. Do not say what happens on the worksheet: Q5 adds 3, and children should look at their own row and say what they see.

l1-ws2.note: Children work alone. Check that each child writes both lists for Q4 and adds 3 to the LAST box for Q5. Note who may need a short catch-up next lesson (never in front of the group).

l1-ws2ans.note: Click each answer after a child explains. Q4b (up to 30 here; the 50 version is Think harder T4): numbers we say in 5s end in 5 or 0; numbers we say in 2s are even; so the shared ones end in 0. Q5: the rule is add 3. Box 10: 26 + 3 = 29. Q5b: adding 3 turns an even number into an odd one and an odd number into an even one, so they take turns. First, everyone stands up and stretches for about a minute (reach up high, touch your toes, shake out your hands) so there is some movement before talk time.

l1-stretch.note: For any pair that chooses to try more (these are on the slide only; Think harder T1 to T4 are in the workbook). Answers: 1) Yes to 39, no to 40 (3, 7, 11, 15, 19, 23, 27, 31, 35, 39, 43: it lands on 39 and jumps over 40). 2) 22 does not belong. It should be 20 (the pattern adds 5). 3) Add 4: from the 3rd to the 5th number is two equal jumps that make 8, and 4 + 4 = 8. The 2nd number is 11 − 4 = 7 and the 1st is 7 − 4 = 3. Check: 3, 7, 11, 15, 19.

l1-challenge.note: For any pair that chooses Go further. Use it as a pair choice, or with volunteers in talk time (never call a child by name). Ask for the reason every time. Q3 is open: there is no single right answer, so ask children to check each other's work. Answers: 1) 29. The gaps are 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, so the 7th is 22 and the 8th is 29. 2) 5, 17, 29 and 41. Each one is 12 more than the one before. 3) Open. Check by writing both lists and ringing the matches. Example: start 2 add 4 (2, 6, 10 …) and start 3 add 3 (3, 6, 9 …) share 6, 18, 30 and 42, with a gap of 12 each time.

l1-chwalk.note: Use after pairs have tried. Reveal one answer at a time and ask a child to explain before you click. Many children stop at one answer: ask "Is there another way?" and "How do you know you found them all?" For Q3, ask two pairs to swap puzzles and solve each other's.

l1-talk.note: Minutes 72 to 79. Pairs talk for 2 minutes. Then ask for volunteers first ("Who would like to share?"), never call a child by name to answer, and say that passing is always fine. No tallies and no rankings. Praise the reasons, not only the answers.

l1-exit.note: Minutes 79 to 85. Answer: 19, 22. Add 3. Extension: Pupils invent a rule (start at 1, add 6) and swap with a partner to find it.

l1-reflect.note: Minutes 85 to 88 (3 minutes, after the exit ticket). Children tick or write the Look-back box on the Choose and look-back page of their workbook. A pass is always allowed. It is never marked, never collected in front of the group and never read out; the tutor may look at it afterwards. If a child ticks "I am still stuck", check in during the open session next lesson (a quick visit to the shared breakout room or a hand signal, with a parent nearby; never a direct message). Do not ask children to share their boxes. Praise the strategy ("Drawing it got you unstuck"), not the speed. The "Next time I will try" row is optional and is never marked; at the start of the next lesson the tutor may say, to the whole group, "Today you could try drawing it, using objects or checking your answer" without naming anyone. Say: "Tick what was hard and what helped you. Write or draw one thing you did well. Then tick one thing you might try next time, if you like. You can pass." After the look-back, minutes 88 to 90 are flex time: the buffer. If the lesson ran late, finish whatever is still open (stamps, the look-back). If you are on time, say goodbye and thank the parents. Do not start anything new.
